entry.title: Curvature-Aware Bezier Curves for Improved Editing
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | acko.net | discussion | hacker news

Standard Bezier curve editing uses symmetric or asymmetric tangents to manage smoothness, but these settings fail to guarantee continuous curvature. This article proposes a system of curvature-aware handles, where handle length is directly proportional to the radius of curvature, to provide a more intuitive and stable editing experience.

The author derives a mathematical approach to solve for tangent lengths using a quadratic system of equations, enabling seamless conversion between traditional Bezier control points and curvature handles. This method helps prevent unexpected curve "popping" and numerical drift during the design process.

entry.title: Qubes OS Security Bulletin 118 Addresses Dom0 Code Execution Vulnerability
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | qubes-os.org | source | hacker news

Qubes Security Bulletin 118 identifies a vulnerability in the `qvm-copy-to-vm` tool that allows a malicious qube to execute arbitrary commands in Dom0. The flaw exists because the error reporting mechanism fails to sanitize shell meta-characters in filenames, which are then passed to a `system()` call during the display of error dialogs.

The vulnerability affects all Qubes OS releases and could allow a compromised qube to take full control of the system. Users are advised to update via the Qubes Update tool; for Qubes 4.3, the fix is being transitioned to the stable repository in the `qubes-core-dom0-linux` version 4.3.22 package.

entry.title: Omarchy Vulnerability Allows Root Escalation via Default Docker Configuration
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | 0xcc.io | source | hacker news

A security flaw in Omarchy's default Docker configuration allows any process running in a user session to escalate privileges to root without a password. By automatically including the default user in the `docker` group, the OS grants processes access to the Docker socket, enabling them to mount host filesystems and execute code with root authority.

This vulnerability affects all versions prior to 4.0.1. Because the `docker` group membership was an opt-out rather than an opt-in feature, common user applications such as web browsers or IDEs could provide a direct path to full system compromise. The issue has been resolved in version 4.0.1 by removing the default group membership.

entry.content:
Hacker News Best | geekyschmidt.com | hacker news

Verschlimmbesserung is a German term describing an attempted improvement that results in a worse outcome. In software development, this often manifests as updates that disrupt established workflows or change user interfaces without providing meaningful value to the user.

These suboptimal updates are often driven by misaligned organizational metrics that reward release frequency and shipping velocity over product stability. When engineering teams are incentivized to prioritize constant delivery over functional utility, they optimize for the metrics provided rather than the actual user experience.

entry.title: TurboKV: An Async Embedded Key-Value Store for Rust
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | github.com | hacker news

TurboKV is an asynchronous, embedded key-value database implemented in Rust. It supports atomic write batches, ordered range scans, and background compaction, with data stored using LZ4, Snappy, or Zstd compression.

The engine provides configurable durability settings through a write-ahead log (WAL), ranging from in-memory visibility to synchronous disk synchronization. It also utilizes hardware-accelerated AES for its Bloom-filter format and allows for various configuration options regarding memory, cache, and compaction.

entry.title: Bug Blindness in Software Development
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | danluu.com | hacker news

Software developers and users often fail to notice significant defects because they have unconsciously adapted to work around them. This cognitive bias can lead teams to believe they are shipping high-quality products even when users encounter severe usability issues or non-functional software.

Common mitigation strategies like "dogfooding" can be undermined if developers have already established habits to bypass problematic workflows. Using Large Language Models to simulate normal users can help identify and reproduce these hidden issues that human developers have become accustomed to.

entry.title: Google Uses a Monolithic Repository to Manage Billions of Lines of Code
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | dl.acm.org | source | discussion

Google manages its massive, centralized codebase through a custom-built version-control system known as Piper. This monolithic repository contains approximately one billion files, two billion lines of code, and 86TB of data, serving as a single source of truth for over 25,000 developers. The system is designed for ultra-large-scale activity, processing billions of file read requests daily and managing millions of weekly changes from both human users and automated systems.

To facilitate efficient development, Google uses "Clients in the Cloud" (CitC), a FUSE-based file system that allows developers to edit files in a cloud-based workspace without the need to clone the entire repository locally. The workflow relies on trunk-based development, where changes are committed to the central mainline to minimize the integration challenges associated with long-lived branches. This model is supported by an extensive automated testing and code-review infrastructure that maintains codebase health amid high commit volumes.
